speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement regarding final payments for barley and oats. Producers delivered 35,104,357 bushels of oats and 106,155,792 bushels of barley to the Canadian Wheat Board in the 1966-67 crop year. The pools for these two crops were closed on January 31. The amounts of the final payments to be distributed are $8,402,616 for oats and a record $35,798,202 for barley.
These are not payments by the government of Canada, but represent the net returns of the Canadian Wheat Board in the marketing of western Canadian oats and barley for the 1966-67 crop year. The board will begin mailing the final payment cheques for barley today, and immediately after completion of the barley payments the final payment cheques for oats will be distributed. The average final payment for barley of 33.7 cents a bushel has been exceeded only once, and the average final payment for oats of 23.9 cents per bushel is just slightly below last year's record payment.
I beg leave, Mr. Speaker, to table the statement being issued today in Winnipeg by the Canadian Wheat Board regarding these final payments.

The 1966-67 wheat pool
account was closed on February 29 and the necessary accounting is now being completed. I expect to be able to make an announcement in about two weeks, when the board will be in a position to commence mailing the final payment cheques for wheat. I may say, however, that through international co-operation toward the implementation of the international grains arrangement scheduled for July 1, the marketing of wheat is now more orderly both as to demand and price.

maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the farmers of western Canada will be pleased to learn that the cheques in payment for oats and barley will be issued soon. Since sales during the past crop year have been much below previous years there is a very serious shortage of cash in the hands of farmers with which to pay the necessary production costs. I might add that as a result of the fact this government has seen fit to contribute greatly to the increased cost of production, these cheques will be most welcome. During the past two years farm costs have risen at an alarming rate, and farmers are caught in a very serious cost-price squeeze.
We are pleased that the final payments on both oats and barley are relatively stable in comparison with past years. However, farmers will be looking forward with great expectations to higher payments on the 1966-67 wheat crop, although I doubt very much if those expectations will be realized.

maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened with interest to the statement just made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. One thing that became obvious very quickly was that in terms of dollars and cents the amount involved to the producers in western Canada was almost identical to that of last year. There has been an increase in deliveries of oats to the board of about 15 million bushels, and there has been an equivalent decline in the deliveries of barley. The amount of the final payment from the board this year comes out to within a cent or two of the amount that was paid last year. It is fair to say, as the last speaker has said, that the cost-price situation in agriculture in western Canada remains acute. The amount incoming in receipts to producers remains relatively static, but meanwhile the cost of production soars.

Clause 5 of C-207 provides for prepayment of the corporation tax. There are different rates of prepayment.

Mr. Speaker, may I draw your attention to the explanatory notes accompanying these clauses in the bills I mentioned. In Bill C-193 the explanatory note for clause 4 reads:
This amendment would require corporations to pay their corporation income tax over a period which commences two months closer to the beginning of their taxation year than at present.
In Bill C-207 the identical words are used in the explanatory note for clause 5. It reads:
This amendment would require corporations to pay their corporation income tax over a period which commences two months closer to the beginning of their taxation year than at present.
In Bill C-208 the explanatory note for clause 2 reads:
This amendment would require corporations to pay their corporation income tax over a period which commences two months closer to the begin-ing of their taxation year than at present.
The person writing the explanatory notes in all three bills was well aware of the fact that they are substantially the same and aimed to accomplish the same objective; that is, that the amendment would require corporations to pay their corporation income tax over a period which commences two months closer to the beginning of their taxation year than at present. I suggest that clause 2 in Bill C-208 violates the rule that we cannot bring back on the floor of the House of Commons a provision which has already been decided by the house.
Since I cannot use the decision of the Speaker to reinforce my own arguments, may I quote the hon. member for Acadia who pointed out yesterday that in a similar decision the Speaker of the day, whom I do not wish to identify, ruled that a clause in the Transportation Act which was previously rejected could not be brought back in an amended form. That ruling bore on a clause. This is a clause of Bill C-208 which I submit contains a provision on which a decision was made on February 19. I have read the similar parts in the explanatory notes, and the end result will be exactly the same. If the payments commence two months closer to the beginning of the taxation year, the end result will be to pay regularly for ten months. I believe this clause 2 should be withdrawn as it appears in the bill before the bill is discussed.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have the opportunity of speaking on Bill No. C-208, as indeed I would have been glad to have the opportunity of speaking on Bill No. C-207 yesterday. The second reading of a bill deals with the principle of the measure, and I hope to discuss that principle and the necessity for this bill within the context of the current financial and economic situation which, in the view of the government, makes a bill of this kind important and necessary at this time.
Amidst the current financial difficulties and problems, and we certainly have them, and the predictions of doom and gloom to come, it is well, Mr. Speaker, to recall the actual and potential strength of this country. This country is one of the richest, most stable and most fortunate countries in the world. It is the envy of practically every other country in the world. It is well also, in order to keep things in perspective, to recall the progress we have made in recent years which puts us in a much stronger position today to meet the difficult problems we are encountering.
The fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada, which was made public in September, 1967, had this to say on page 11 in the section dealing with the performance of the economy. In this paragraph the council was referring to the expansion since 1961:
This represents probably the longest uninterrupted expansion-and certainly the longest peacetime expansion-in Canadian business cycle history.
[Mr. Speaker.)

The governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Speaker, also mentioned the economic gains we have made, while warning us in very clear terms of the dangers and difficulties ahead, in a speech which he made last November in Winnipeg. Referring again to the period of the last six years, he said:
Our real output has increased by over 40 per cent and we have greatly strengthened the economic foundations of the country. We have added greatly to our manufacturing capacity and demonstrated our ability to sell more manufactured goods in world markets. We have continued to seek out and develop a wide variety of forest and mineral and power resources. We have added significantly to our infrastructure in the form of roads and other means of transportation. We have provided greatly increased facilities for general and technical education. And at the same time as we have done all these things we have raised our standard of living rapidly: Personal consumption per head has risen by nearly a quarter since the beginning of this decade.
Then, he went on:
Our basic problem is how to cope with prosperity and add to high levels of output already attained: Our present difficulties do not arise out of any basic economic weakness or shortage of resources-
Mr. Rasminsky then pointed out that by 1966 it was clear that our growth rate would decrease, and that the main question was whether this would take place without the expansion coming to a full stop as has happened so often in similar circumstances in the past. In fact, as matters turned out, economic expansion has continued, though at a distinctly more moderate and sustainable rate. In other words, bust has not followed boom. It is undeniable, however, that we are now facing serious economic and financial problems, but so is every country in the world including the United Kingdom and the United States.
It is true also that these problems are made more dangerous, and their solutions made more difficult, by threats to the international financial and economic co-operation which so far has distinguished the post-war years from those of the thirties. It is devoutly to be hoped that we do not return to those earlier years when governments foolishly thought they could save themselves by adopting protectionist national policies which attempted to export their own difficulties and their own problems. Today, the reversion to economic nationalism of that kind would only compound every country's difficulties and lead the
March 12, 1968

way to general economic and political deterioration which could be fatal to international progress and co-operation.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, has played, and hopes to continue to play, a full part in international economic co-operation, particularly in the international trade and payments system that has been built up and which, as we have learned to our advantage recently, is still working despite the intense strains to which it is currently subjected and which could destroy it with unhappy results.
Canada's own basic position, as I have said, is strong, and so is the backing for our dollar. If anyone feels pessimistic about the situation in Canada, let him read this report which came out the day before yesterday from the O.E.C.D., which is an international committee, and which deals with the current economic and financial situation in Canada. Our economic and financial position has stood up well, then, to the pressures which have been directed against it, as indeed they have been directed against other countries. In so far as standing up to those pressures is concerned, I should like to pay my tribute and give thanks to the government of the United States for the way it has co-operated with Canada in meeting those pressures in a way which is of advantage to both countries.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that no country, certainly no country in the position of Canada, can isolate itself from those pressures which are continuing but which by their very nature make sound national policies more important than ever. We have our own responsibilities to discharge and we will not be excused for failure to do so by blaming that failure on the international situation, on the exchange gamblers, on Paris or on Viet Nam. However, Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that our financial problems today, as is the case with other countries, are being increasingly aggravated by troubled international situations both economic and political.
The problem of most immediate concern to us, Mr. Speaker, is to maintain financial stability without hindering economic expansion. This is more and more difficult to accomplish in an age of rising costs, rising expenditures and rising expectations. While government policies do require heavy public expenditures at all levels of government-and I will have something to say about that a little later -they also increasingly require the determination of priorities, again at all levels of government, in the allocation of resources.
Income Tax Act
This is the more necessary and the more difficult, Mr. Speaker, because conditions, both national and international, change so rapidly these days. It is not easy to adapt economic and financial policies to those changes. I do not think we need to be smug or complacent as to our own successes or failures, if you like, in regard to this adaptation. But I would quote from the report of this international body, the O.E.C.D., which had this to say at page 12:
A striking feature of the last two years has been the speed with which policies-
They are writing about Canadian policies.
-have been adjusted to changes in business conditions. And in most cases the timing and magnitude of the policy measures adopted was well chosen.
Again on page 31, in the conclusion of the report, there is this paragraph:
In the last two years, with the trend of business conditions changing quickly, the authorities-
They are referring to the Canadian authorities.
-have on the whole been successful in maintaining relatively high levels of employment while combating first excesses and then mildly recessionary tendencies appearing on the demand side. Both monetary and fiscal policies have been rather promptly adjusted to changing conditions.
Our most worrying problem at the present time, as I have just said, Mr. Speaker, is the threat to financial stability from the recent and continuing rates of increase of prices, incomes and costs in the Canadian economy. The steps that have been taken in fiscal and monetary policy now need to be supplemented by new procedures to ensure that the public interest in price stability is taken into account whenever important decisions affecting prices, incomes and costs are made.
Before dealing with these measures, Mr. Speaker, I wish to review the background against which these procedures that will be recommended should be viewed. In a white paper on employment and income in 1945 the government of Canada committed itself-and successive governments have accepted that commitment-to the maintenance of a high and stable level of employment. Henceforth that was to be a central objective of economic policy in this country, and rightly so.
While this objective was not always fulfilled, Mr. Speaker, during the years that followed, we did have two long periods of sustained growth and high employment. Of course, employment is directly related to

March 12. 1968
Income Tax Act
growth. That is why we had high employment, because we had the growth. This situation prevailed until the recession of the late fifties which was succeeded after 1961 by a renewed steady growth of production and employment.
There is also a direct relationship, in economic growth, between productivity and the level of real income. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of this relationship it is very disturbing to all members, I think, to realize that now the average productivity of the Canadian worker is still appreciably less than that of his counterpart in the United States. I am sure that all members will agree that this situation must be corrected if Canadians wish to enjoy living standards equal or nearer to those of Americans. Increases in productivity is essential if we are to have rising incomes without the kind of inflation which will rapidly erode the benefits we would otherwise receive from this rise.
Price inflation works great inequities, causing the greatest hardship to the relatively weak groups in the community who have no organized market power to combat it, those whose incomes are fixed or lag well behind the increasing cost of living. When price inflation persists long enough and creates a general expectation of further inflation, then serious distortions arise in the whole economy as well as in financial markets. The likely consequence is recession and large scale unemployment. This is particularly true in a country like Canada because our economic well-being depends so greatly on our international competitive position. When our prices rise faster than those of the United States, in particular, and of our other major trading partners, we are in trouble. That is why I was very glad to read in this O.E.C.D. report the following sentence on page 31:
There is little indication that the competitive position of Canadian industry has yet been seriously impaired.

Yes. It has been impaired, but this publication says that it has not yet been seriously impaired. As my hon. friend realizes, Mr. Speaker, I am not underestimating the difficulties that may cause that serious impairment unless we do something about them. Price stability is a necessary condition for achieving the other goals of high employment and adequate growth.
The responsibility of government to curb inflation is made the more difficult because

financial and currency problems are often concerned with considerations that are more psychological than concrete in nature. The problem of psychology is largely one of confidence.
There are some who appear to believe that prices and costs will continue rising in the way they have in recent months. They assume that further inflation is inevitable and thereby help to make it so. This is dangerous, of course, because inflation feeds on itself. Moreover, while some, and rightly, may fear it, others may find it good because of the feeling of prosperity and well-being it may give for a time. It can produce an l.s.d. experience-and I am not talking about pounds, shillings and pence. So government has a responsibility to do what it can to prevent the "hangover" by preventing the experience.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
During the period of economic expansion which began in 1961 we had for most of that time reasonable price stability. This brought great benefits to all Canadians and demonstrated the underlying strength of our economy. It also, as I have said, brought problems of prosperity, prices and cost problems, arising out of the growing strains in recent years on our resources. Looking back in retrospect, it is clear that dangerous upward pressures on prices and costs were going to be hard to avoid, but that was not so clear at the time. In its second annual review, published in December, 1965, the Economic Council of Canada was still in a position to say, and I quote from the report of the council published in that month:
-a careful appraisal of the nature and patterns of recent changes would suggest that at the present time there appears to be little evidence to indicate that a broad and widely dispersed acceleration of price increases or accentuation of price pressures is under way.
That is what the economic council said at the end of 1965. However, as the economy subsequently moved to even higher levels of employment and heavier pressures on our resources, price inflation at that time became, and it remains, a major danger. It was then that monetary and fiscal action was taken by the government to moderate demands on our resources.
Despite the easing of pressures in the economy, Canada's price performance over the last year or two, in contrast with earlier years, has been bad. It now compares
March 12, 1968

unfavourably with that of most other industrialized countries and, of special significance to us, it compares unfavourably with that of the United States of America.
The average annual rate of increase in the consumer price index from January, 1965, to January, 1968, has been 3.7 per cent. From 1952 to 1965 it was only 1.3 per cent. During the whole period from 1949 to 1967, the rate was 2.3 per cent. So our recent performance has not been good.
It is important to note also that prices of imported goods have not been increasing more rapidly in the past three years than in the period 1952 to 1964. Obviously any marked increase in import prices can exert strong upward leverage on domestic price levels, as happened, for example, in 1950-51. But this has not been the case this time. The average annual increase in import prices has been 1.3 per cent from the beginning of 1965 to the third quarter of 1967, compared with an average annual rate of 1.7 per cent from 1952 to 1964.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, prices of most types of goods and services have recently been rising at rates that are clearly inconsistent with any definition of reasonable price stability.
Productivity, of course, is an important factor in these matters; it is an important determinant of prices and income. The only way to increase real incomes, with a given quantity of capital and labour, is to improve productivity. Increases of money incomes which run ahead of increases of real output are, for the country as a whole, illusory and self-defeating. So policies to achieve price stability must be policies to keep the over-all increase in incomes within limits set by the real increase in production.
The urgency of this matter, and it is urgent, is shown, among other things, by the fact that in the past two years new wage settlements have on the average provided for annual increases in earnings of more than 8 per cent. The O.E.C.D. report which I referred to put it at 8.7 per cent. Such increases are well beyond the long-run average gain in productivity in Canada, by any relevant measure. They are also well above the increases in the last two years under similar collective agreements in the United States, where long-run average productivity growth is about the same as in Canada.
Corporation profits, which in the early years of expansion had risen strongly to relatively high levels, have, however, declined

significantly in the course of the past two years. Profits before tax in 1967 were about 5 per cent lower than two years earlier, although non-farm output had increased by some 8 to 9 per cent. Without this decline in profits-and I admit that the decline has been from the high levels of the earlier period- wage and salary increases in excess of productivity gains would have had an even greater effect on prices.
This spiralling process in prices and incomes cannot be halted overnight, but we must do our best to check it. There is no easy way to do this in a free society and in an open economy, and Canada has about the most open economy in the world. There is no easy way to do this, especially in a period of economic expansion. Rising demands, which go with expansion and prosperity, push up costs. Rising costs push up prices. Higher prices in their turn further push up costs, which affect production and consumption and halt expansion.
For the resulting difficulties, labour blames big business and management and their excessive profits. Big business blames labour unions and their alleged excessive demands. Consumers blame the merchants. The merchants blame the manufacturers, and everyone blames the government, especially the federal government, even though more than 55 per cent of the taxes in this country now go to provincial and municipal governments.
These days I receive letters, listen to speeches and read editorials in the newspapers urging the government to cut expenditures, to reduce inflationary pressures and lower rising costs. However, the government is also urged, often by the same people who demand that we cut costs, to spend more money on pensions, on anti-pollution measures, on housing, on price supports for farmers, on education, retraining, health grants, research and on a great many other worthy and important projects and purposes. Every day we are urged to curb expenditures. At the same time we are criticized for cutting out or cutting down on some good and favourite projects, even though it is realized that in present circumstances some very desirable things will have to be postponed or scrapped or reduced in order to keep the finances of the country on an even keel.
Eventually everything has to be paid for and the government does not have any magic way of raising money for these purposes. It

I will come to that in a few moments. I will show who is taking the lead in cutting expenditures.
The government has to spend the money it collects wisely and well, of course, but that money can only be secured by taxing or borrowing. At the present time it is not easy to do either-either to tax or to borrow. Interest rates make it difficult to borrow and taxes are already high. But the money must be found and that is one of the purposes of the bill before the house. We cannot safely indulge in deficit financing when inflation, not recession, is the main danger.
To check inflation government must, of course, keep its own financial affairs in order. This requires in present circumstances establishing a balance between income and expenditure even if it means the postponement or elimination for the time being of many good projects and the reduction of government borrowing even for good purposes. We are eliminating certain programs and we have postponed or stretched out others.
We have reduced substantially the amount we shall have to spend as well as the amounts

we shall have to borrow in 1968 for all purposes. We have asked the provincial governments and, through them, municipal governments, to co-operate in this effort. Reduction of expenditures and an increase in revenues, along with a reduction of non-budgetary outlays, are, then, necessary for financial stability. This, I repeat, is why we have introduced the bill now before the house and why we shall propose further cuts in expenditure.
The critics of the government say, of course, that there ought not to be any tax increases, or that the kind we are proposing are the wrong kind; that our proposals are inflationary or that they are deflationary; sometimes these two complaints are made in the course of the same speech. They say the reductions are made in the wrong places, or that they should not be made at all, or that the reductions should be bigger. The government is accused of being niggardly or extravagant, or both.
The most persistent charge is that we have lost control of expenditures, which are said to be skyrocketing. I submit that the government has made a very real and effective effort to maintain control over increased expenditure.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE

Such control, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) quite rightly said some time ago, is the only control which in present conditions is realistic. Our effort has certainly been more successful in controlling expenditure than the effort made at the provincial and municipal levels as comparative figures show quite clearly. We are now achieving a substantial reduction in the rate of increase in budgetary expenditures. The rate of increase for 1968-69 will be 4.1 per cent. It was 12.5 per cent for the current fiscal year. On October 4 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), as reported on page 2810 of Hansard, told the House of Commons of our efforts to screen and reduce programs and expenditures and work toward a balanced budget. The opposition was not impressed. They claimed that federal expenditures remained excessive and were out of control and getting more so in comparison with the growth of our national product, and that we have no right to ask for taxes until we have reduced expenditures to much lower levels.
Let me give the house some figures to show that the percentage increase in federal expenditures, was not greater but less than the increase in the gross national product during
March 12, 1968

Income Tax Act
the last five years. There was a 42 per cent increase in the gross national product as against 30 per cent in federal expenditures. During the period from 1957 to 1966, roughly a ten-year period, the increase in federal expenditures and the increase in the gross national product were roughly the same-81 per cent. But during the same period the increase in provincial and municipal expenditures amounted to 186 per cent. For the ten-year period as a whole, the percentage increase in federal expenditures was identical with the increase in the gross national product. In that same period the annual average percentage increase in provincial and municipal expenditures was 12.1, while the average annual increase in federal expenditures was 6.7 per cent, and we shall be reducing that in the forthcoming year to 4.1 per cent.
The same trend is shown in the figures for total federal and provincial expenditures as percentages of the gross national product. In 1954 federal expenditure represented 16.9 per cent of the g.n.p. That figure in the first three-quarters of 1967 had gone down to 14.5 per cent whereas the figure for provincial and municipal expenditure had risen from 10.7 per cent to 19.4 per cent.
Equally significant are the percentage figures of total public expenditures in Canada divided between the federal government on the one hand and provincial and municipal governments on the other. In 1952 the federal percentage was 66 per cent. This had declined by 1966 to 43 per cent whereas provincial and municipal expenditure had gone up from 34 per cent to 57 per cent. I am not criticizing the increased requirements of the provinces and the municipal governments. They were, of course, required for important things. But these figures do indicate where the impact of expenditure mainly lies at the present time in terms of prices and costs. The figures tell their own story.
I should like to look at the total federal expenditure figures in more detail and consider why these have been increasing in recent years. Our budgetary expenditures in 1962-63 amounted to $6,570 billion. The projected figure for the current year is $9,885 billion. This represents an increase in roughly a five-year period of $3,315 billion. Next year we are budgeting for $10.3 billion which we hope to reduce by $75 million.
Now what was the nature of the expenditure involved in this figure of $9,885 billion which has been described as extravagant and as representing an excessive increase over
preceding years? Of this amount $1,800 million is allocated to defence. This represents 18.2 per cent of our budget and 2.9 per cent of our gross national product. It is the lowest percentage of the gross national product devoted to defence by any country in NATO except Denmark and Luxembourg. Can we reduce it? Of course we can, if we wish to withdraw from our present commitments for collective and continental defence, if we wish to withdraw from the Atlantic coalition for defence-

The second great category of expenditures in this total of over $9 billion represents payments to individuals in this country. Among them are pensions, family and youth allowances, the government contribution to unemployment insurance, and veterans pensions. These total $2,428 million.
The third category is payments to provincial governments, and this year they represent $1,892 million. These are total figures, and that is where our money is going.
Let us now look at the increases, both the amount of the increases in absolute terms and the nature of them. The first category of increases is to be found in programs introduced by the present government which represented new expenditures in 1967-68. In that year expenditures for these new programs came to $424 million.
What are these new programs? They include youth allowances, the health resources fund, the fund for rural economic development, occupational training for adults, which cost $120 million, the municipal development and loan board, post-secondary educational grants, which cost $103 million, manpower mobility, the Canada Student Loans Act, the area development program, the program for advancement of industrial technology, defence industry modernization, and general incentives to industry for the expansion of scientific research and development in Canada. All these represent a $424 million increase for very good proposals and projects.
The second category of increases covers increases in the last five years in programs

Income Tax Act
which have been enlarged by the present government. These programs include family allowances, old age, blind, disabled and unemployment assistance, the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, medical research grants, subsidies and other payments to provinces, payments to municipalities, veterans affairs, freight assistance, the trans-Canada highway. Over that period these increases come to $1,075 million.
If you look at the increases over a one-year period you will find that the main increase last year in the categories of health and welfare for increased social security, debt charges, provincial and municipal governments, veterans affairs, transportation and communications, resources development and Indian affairs, aid to education, external aid and general government expenditures, which was only a $20 million increase, came to an over-all total of $975 million. Surely the increases in expenditures last year were on programs and projects which had good and worthy ends.
In this connection I would like to point out two things. The first is that of our total expenditures more than 55 per cent are uncontrollable. The second is that some of the biggest increases within the last few years have been under such things as the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the family allowances programs. The increases with respect to these programs are automatic with the increases in population. Those automatic increases have amounted to $124 million this year, which could be added to those over which the government cannot exercise control because of the nature of the expenditures themselves.
Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in our expenditures to an extent never exceeded before in this country we have been relating economic policies and social policies. This is one of the things that has got us into some financial difficulty and why we now have to use the instruments of economic policy perhaps a little more effectively than we have been doing for the last year or two.
These instruments of economic policy, which the house knows are used to influence our economy, are fiscal policy and monetary policy. They are both powerful instruments. The federal government and the central bank-and here I want to pay my tribute to the way the central bank has been managing its affairs-have tried to employ these instruments as effectively as possible in the difficult and changing circumstances that they have

had to face. Yet these instruments do have their limitations. There is no doubt about that.
The impact of both monetary and fiscal policies on the level of demand in the economy is not immediate but takes effect with a very significant time lag, and that means that those policies have to be formulated with a forward view of the economy. But the economy, especially in these days, is often subject to influences that are essentially unpredictable and that make accurate forecasting very difficult indeed. The techniques of economic forecasting have improved considerably over the years but there will always remain unpredictable situations, as pointed out in the report of the O.E.C.D. to which I have referred.
There will always be the risk that the combined weight of monetary and fiscal policy will be inappropriate at some particular period of time. This risk is greatest when the economy is already operating at high levels of output and employment and when a moderate under-estimation of future demand strength may be sufficient to permit the emergence of excessive demand pressure. The reverse mistake could also be made and lead to recession.
Therefore the government has supplemented fiscal and monetary policies by selective economic programs of a longer range importance, designed to improve productivity, to encourage price competition within the economy, and to make it easier for workers to move to the jobs where they are most needed.
Among these are the programs for occupational training and retraining, the labour mobility program, the program for the advancement of industrial technology, industrial research and development incentives, the rural development program and the adjustment assistance programs. The government has also made very substantial funds available to the provinces for vocational, technical and professional education.
These selective programs, along with fiscal and monetary policies, have their effect over the longer term. But in the current situation additional measures are required to have a more direct and immediate effect. We must find some effective means of influencing, not controlling but influencing, the many individual decisions that give rise to increases in incomes, costs and prices. To this end the government proposes to establish a governmental agency, commission or board, whatever it may be called, to review and scrutinize
March 12, 1968

major decisions affecting prices, incomes and costs throughout the economy.
This agency will analyse the nature and probable effect of such decisions and, where necessary, subject them to public review and criticism. It will also discuss price and cost problems with representatives of management, labour and consumers, in order to clarify the issues involved and ensure before major decisions are reached that all concerned are aware of the issues and that in dealing with them the public interest is taken fully into account.
The precise nature and the terms of reference of this review agency will be determined after necessary consultations with interested parties. These include provincial governments, the leading elements in the labour movement and in industry, professional associations and others concerned. We shall also, Mr. Speaker, take carefully into account any views on this proposal expressed in parliament.
Consultation with and the co-operation of the provinces will be of first importance. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that except for businesses and operations under federal jurisdiction, prices, incomes and costs are matters largely within provincial jurisdiction.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Of course the federal government has responsibility for fiscal and monetary policy. But to avoid any conflict or misunderstanding the agency's legal functions, which we propose, will be limited to inquiry and report and to the focusing of public opinion on the findings it may make, compliance with which will be voluntary.
There are various ways in which such a prices and costs review agency could be established. But it is important that it should be done quickly and I believe this can be done by using the provisions of the Inquiries Act. It is not contemplated, therefore, that additional legislation will be required at this time. In the light of experience, if and when an agency with greater powers and authority is required-and this is the way such a board was handled in the United Kingdom-then the government can submit legislation to parliament for that purpose within the constitutional authority it has. Meanwhile action can be taken under the Inquiries Act at once to set up this machinery with carefully defined powers of investigation and report.
Income Tax Act
In connection with the role of any review agency it is interesting to look at the course adopted in the United Kingdom and followed by the government of the United Kingdom through the national board for prices and incomes. There the problem is a simpler one constitutionally, of course, than we have in Canada. According to an official United Kingdom statement the policy objective of the government in setting up that board was that "money incomes should rise in line with the long term growth of national output and that a generally stable level of prices should be maintained." The specific role of the board is "to examine and report on any questions relating to prices charged for goods or services; to pay claims or settlements or other matters relating to conditions of service and employment; or to any other form of income." The British board has interpreted its task as having three aims: "First, to bring home to the parties immediately concerned the wider implications of their actions; second, to bring these implications home to others involved in similar situations which are not before the board; third, as promoting a quicker adaptation of out of date practices to new needs through consultation between management, unions and the government." In Canada we will have the advantage of working out the powers of this review agency after studying the experience of the United Kingdom board which has been in operation now since 1965, I think.
In the United States similar responsibilities have been assigned to a cabinet committee on price stability which recently has been established. Many other countries have set up similar agencies or agencies with a similar purpose in mind. The methods adopted in other countries have varied but it is clear that machinery of this kind is found to be essential in many major industrial countries.
As an immediate step to deal with the problem in Canada pending the establishment of the board or agency or commission, a special ad hoc committee of cabinet composed of certain ministers who have responsibility in these matters is being established and charged with the responsibility of ensuring that effective action is taken jointly to develop and bring this program into effect. I have sent letters to the premiers of the provinces setting out our concern about the problem, our ideas concerning how we should proceed to deal with it and asking for their co-operation. We are proposing early meetings

between federal and provincial representatives to discuss in detail the way in which the two levels of government can co-operate most effectively in this important task. A small group of senior officials is getting in touch with the provincial governments to prepare the way for these early consultations.

I would think the authority of the agency in its investigatory powers under the act would be sufficient for that purpose.
Canada is by no means alone in having to face the problem of reconciling full employment with the maintenance of reasonable stability of prices. Other countries have resolved this objective through a variety of means, but it is urgent that Canada find methods that fit the Canadian political, constitutional and economic framework. We must deal effectively with the problem because a solution must be found to it if we are to proceed with sustained economic expansion.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the house to look at the bill before it in the light of current financial conditions as well as in the light of the background of the other conditions which I have ventured to put forward and with which perhaps I have dealt at too great length. I have no hesitation in the circumstances we face to ask the house to support this bill. It represents only a part but an important part of the government's plans. These must be plans at all levels of government in order to secure for this country financial stability with an economic expansion that is continuous and sustainable, the benefits of which will be shared fully and fairly among all sections of our people.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister permit one short question? In the light of the action now taken by the government can he explain why while campaigning in Quebec the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) spoke of reducing the tax burden on the Canadian people rather than increasing it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: I hope the time will come, Mr. Speaker, when that may be done. Perhaps the minister was looking into the future.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this government has introduced more strange and undesirable parliamentary precedents than all its predecessors put together. This afternoon another has been added-a budget by instalments. Last week we had budgets by press conference and budgets by television. This afternoon we have a budget by instalments. Last Wednesday the minister announced new budgetary measures to replace those defeated by the house. He announced them in committee of supply. Today, just four parliamentary days later, we have the unusual spectacle of the Prime Minister, in what is probably his parliamentary swan song, delivering another budget message. By what procedure? He intervenes on second reading to make a statement which is in fact irrelevant to the bill under discussion. The only way to describe this inept and bumbling procedure is "budget by instalments".

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE

One thing that is clear, sir, is that this government of alleged decision has been demonstrated to be a government of ineptitude. For, sir, this new budget which was delivered by the Prime Minister was really an admission of failure. It is an apologia for the fact that the Prime Minister acknowledges at last "that Canada's price performance over the past year or two has been bad". It has been bad, Mr. Speaker. That is what we have been trying to tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance for months and months on end. Deaf to our pleas have they been. The Prime Minister went on to say: "It now compares unfavourably with that of most other industrialized countries and, of special significance, with that of the United States." Mr. Speaker, that sounds as if the Leader of the Opposition had written it.
March 12, 1968

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
What is the Prime Minister's remedy lor the situation? The substance of his parliamentary swan song today was apparently a prices and income review agency or commission. He has not even decided what it is to be called; that is a token of the significance he attaches to it. He says an agency or a commission, or call it what you will. Its functions, its objectives and particularly its procedures and its sanctions were left vague and uncertain. The conclusion I came to as I listened to the Prime Minister was that the proposal was a tangled and belated compromise between expediency and necessity.
Certainly inflationary pressures throughout the nation are rampant. Firm and decisive action is imperative. The savings of our people have been eroded and continue to be eroded month by month. Gains in wages have been lost due to fantastic price increases, even before wage earners have had an opportunity to enjoy them. Up and up has gone the cost of living and down and down has gone employment. Today, for example, in our greatest city, Montreal, the unemployment rate is 7 per cent, which represents an unemployed working force larger than the total working force of the capital of Saskatchewan, the city of Regina. Those who are employed are living in dread and fear of runaway inflation. Why do we have these situations in this great country? I am going to analyse some of the reasons the Prime Minister advanced this afternoon but I say to him directly, and I say what the people of Canada know, that the basic reason lies with the 27 men who sit opposite of the treasury benches.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext:
Mismanagement of
our economy, mistaken budgetary and fiscal policies, fire and fall back policies, flip flop -these have been the characteristics displayed by the Prime Minister and his band of quarrelsome, querulous colleagues. Make no mistake, it is this government which is the author of our economic misfortune, and no attempt to blame it on international factors or blame it on the provinces or municipalities has any basic realism. Excessive spending, wasteful practices, and blindness to economic forces have brought us to the brink of disaster. No attention has been paid to the warnings of the Economic Council of Canada and less to the Auditor General's reports. Politics first has been the watchword of this government.
Income Tax Act
Will this belated attempt to impose some restraint be of any value? I think the Canadian people will insist on something more than window-dressing. They have been fed enough political flim-flam and economic humbug. Look at the situation. Last June the Minister of Finance talked about guide lines and then he backed away from them. He abandoned this procedure of persuasive restraint. Today, nine months later, what does the government do? It suggests, and I think this is the sum total of the Prime Minister's speech this afternoon, that at some later date it may lock the stable door after it has investigated to make sure that the horse has really been stolen.
What about this matter of priorities that the Prime Minister suggests? What a conversion that is, Mr. Speaker. Not since the conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus has there been anything to equal the Prime Minister's new rectitude in this clasping to his breast of the very policy of priorities that he has always spurned. Priorities indeed. I really thought that only we on this side of the house had talked in that realistic manner. He says, "Oh, yes, we are going to establish an ad hoc committee of the cabinet". How that will make the profiteers tremble. Sir, if a cabinet committee frightens industry and labour as much as any form of a committee of this cabinet frightens the members of this house, inflation will be over automatically,
What of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs? Some of us on this side of the house were under the illusion that it was established to do the very things that are now suggested are going to be done by this agency, commission or call it what you will. Is it that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) is in the doghouse because of his leadership ambitions? Must his wings be clipped? Is this why the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is being denuded of all those great things described to us earlier in the session as its role? What is to happen with all the officials who have been appointed to this new department? The Prime Minister left this unsaid, but merely inferred the transfer of authority to the new agency, commission or call it what you will.
The absence of genuine effectiveness in the new proposal the Prime Minister made this afternoon would seem to be indicated by the fact that no legislation is proposed by the government, that the existing legislative powers are sufficient. "We will do it under the

March 12, 1968
Income Tax Act
Inquiries Act." If parliament can be bypassed now let me point out that the government had it in its power to establish this commission or agency at any time in the last 18 or 24 months when the inflationary situation was developing. The Prime Minister said this afternoon that conditions had been bad during the last two years. That was his phrase, "bad for two years". Why then, if he admits that today, did he dilly-dally and fiddle while the flames of inflation developed?
The Prime Minister gave no indication this afternoon whether there would be any sanctions in this agency or commission. What teeth will it have? Will it be merely a toothless albatross encumbering the economy? The Prime Minister, as I say, does not even know what it should be called. Whatever it may be called, will it be merely the establishment of another cumbersome, ineffective bureaucracy to replace the jurisdiction of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who now appears to have got himself in the doghouse?
At the moment the government's proposal, I submit, is nothing more than an expression of pious future intention. The government cannot make up their minds what to do, so they ask others to tell them. I suggest that these pious intentions look just like buckpassing. There are many questions that must be answered before the attitude of this house to the proposal in respect of this particular agency can be determined.
We on this side of the house, and let me make this absolutely clear, are determined that inflation must be stopped, but we have had enough of gay promises without any subsequent effective action. Perhaps there are two things about which I might congratulate the Prime Minister. First, he made a speech in the House of Commons and not on television. Second, at long last he recognized that the present economic expansion started in the year 1961. Listen to his phrase this afternoon, of which I made very careful note-"during our period of expansion which began in 1961". How different from what he used to say when he sat on this side of the house and when the speeches were rolled out for him by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen). Only because the Prime Minister is about to leave us do I refrain from saying that it has taken the right hon. member for Algoma East at least three years to destroy the expansion of the economy which the Progressive Conservative government began.

[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
May I now give some attention to the new income tax bill, the third attempt at legislative parenthood by the Minister of Finance. This now emasculated bill is the crumbling cornerstone of the government's tottering budgetary edifice. Allegedly the tax increases which it contains-and that is all that is left of it-are designed to meet the fiscal, economic and international crisis which was once so fervently denied by the government but is now so clearly admitted on all sides as well as by the Prime Minister this afternoon.
This crisis is chiefly of the government's own creation. But I want to put to the house very directly that the real crisis in Canada today is a crisis of government, or more specifically a crisis due to lack of competent government. Whatever tinkering may be attempted by fiscal and budgetary expedients, whatever piecemeal efforts may be made to bolster our sagging economy, the crisis will not be ended until this incompetent government is dismissed by the electors. It will not be ended until the government is replaced by a responsible, effective and decisive administration. Yes, sir, the crisis in Canada today is a crisis of confidence and confidence, both domestic and international, can only be restored by a new government.
I think Strickland Gillilan must have had this government in mind when he wrote:
Off ag'in, on ag'in,
Gone ag'in-Finnigan.
What other seven words could more aptly describe the fiscal and economic gyrations of the Minister of Finance? I suggest that his words have seldom been matched by actions, and such actions as he has taken have misfired or been reversed. Unlike any of his predecessors, the Minister of Finance has permitted himself to be the prisoner of events, instead of attempting to act as the captain of the nation's fiscal fate. Yet in his rather frequent television appearances-and I do not attach anything sinister to the number of times he has been on television recently-the Minister of Finance has developed a unique talent for making his inconsistency sound plausible and his about-turns appear economically sophisticated as well as personal vindications.
This house realizes that this is the sixth income tax bill in two sessions of parliament. This country has been treated to the spectacle of what amounts to four budgets in just over 14 months. The first one was on December 19,
March 12, 1968



1966, the second on June 1, 1967, the third on November 30, 1967, and the fourth on March 6, 1968, which now has been extended by this procedure of budgets by instalments. Of course, as we all know, there have been some intermediate so-called financial statements. The Minister of Finance has done at least one thing. He has achieved an all-time record as a budgeter within the briefest possible period. I suggest to the house that that fact in itself constitutes a confession of dismal failure and of unprecedented fiscal mismanagement. The minister says, "Oh no, this demonstrates flexibility". Flexibility, as the minister interprets it, is just an excuse for uncertainty and a cover for inadequate foresight or the total failure of any foresight.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Chretien) was very clear about this. I thought he made one of the frankest presentations on television on Sunday night that I have ever heard. The interviewer's name was Mr. Martin, and I do not think it was the hon. member for Essex East. Mr. Martin asked the following question in discussing the manner in which the budget was presented:
And yet, generally enough, in the press it has been recognized as a sort of contempt of parliament.
This is what the Minister of National Revenue answered, and I quote from a translation on which I had the skilled assistance of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert):
Oh well, some people! There are many traditionalists in Canada and Mr. Sharp is not one of them. He is an extremely flexible person, so flexible that in fact it is his third budget. He is not wedded to the idea that one must present a budget and be bound by it. One must follow economic circumstances, and it is not something very wrong.
The Minister of National Revenue is apparently a great one to make a virtue out of necessity. He said that the Minister of Finance is so flexible that in fact he has delivered three budgets. Flexible, indeed. Let us imagine that instead of making three mistakes he had made six. If he had delivered six budgets he would have been even more flexible. Is fiscal uncertainty to be elevated to a principle of statecraft?
The Minister of Finance has attempted to justify his various changes of course and pace by alleging international factors, as did the Prime Minister this afternoon. But I ask the Prime Minister and I ask the Minister of Finance: Can they point to any nation which has followed such an uncertain, inconsistent
Income Tax Act
budgetary policy as to need four budgets in 14 months?
In the first of these budgets the minister urged restraint. In the second he expressed fear that restraints might lead to recession or economic slowdown. In the third he reversed himself again and asserted a renewed need for restraints, and in the present budget measures he has simply reiterated or underlined that need. In the first budget he taxed, then he removed taxes, then he reversed himself and taxed again, and now in this bill he has proposed another form of taxation. Surely nothing more is needed to establish that the minister has simply resembled a cork bobbing in the economic sea, helpless to resist the waves and helpless to resist forces which he neither foresaw nor attempted to control in advance.
The Prime Minister quoted various alleged authorities this afternoon but he forgot to quote the words of the London Economist written on September 30, 1967, which focus attention on the failure of our fiscal policies as represented by this bill as vividly today as they did then. They read as follows:
Mr. Sharp, alas, cannot avoid the responsibility for inadequate fiscal action, the need for which he now seems belatedly to have realized. His budget-
That is the June budget.
-did not revive last year's expansion, but it did nothing to stem the rise in costs and prices. Worst of all, it pushed interest rates higher, because the public was unwilling to absorb bonds and generate a further increase in the money supply.
There we have stated what is responsible for the outrageous interest rates in this country today, namely, the policies of this government which have pushed interest rates higher. The article reads further:
There have been few examples of such a violent swing of the levers of economic control. Policies that would have been admirably suited to cope with a state of excessive under-utilization of resources were continued well after demand was clearly pressing too hard on the limits of supply. This was not the fault of business, which was trying to cope with its own cost squeeze, but the fault of government which ought to have been far more sensitive to the signals that the economy was making to it.
There, exposed by perhaps the most perceptive economic journal in the world, is the record of the fiscal flip-flop which has led us to our present crisis and which is the parent of this bill. The Economist pinpoints the undoubted fact that government policies are responsible for the usurious interest rates

March 12, 1968
Income Tax Act
crippling the economy, interest rates which simply cannot be continued at their present level. It pinpoints as well the violent changes in government policy. This article, which as I say is as penetrating and perceptive today as it was in September, concludes with this comment:
What Canada needs is not a change in the country's longer term objective of well-based prosperity, but the simple recognition that the pace of spending has been running ahead of real output.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Well, sir, the government's recognition of this fact has been to increase this year's main estimates as contrasted with last year's main estimates by almost 8 per cent. I am going to deal with the Prime Minister's figures in this respect. Restraint is what the government preaches, but extravagance and wastefulness are what it practices. In his statement this afternoon the Prime Minister said that the increase in the estimates this year was 4.1 per cent over last year. I suggest that this figure is simply a delusion. It compares apples with oranges. It compares next year's main estimates with the total of all of this year's estimates. It is a phony technique of argument.
This comparison gives no consideration whatever to the supplementary estimates, no consideration to the expenditures that will be required for medicare. I say to you that the only realistic figure to put forward in any comparison of the main estimates for next year would be an increase of almost 8 per cent over last year's main estimates. There is the Expo deficit and a variety of other things to consider. Before we are finished the increase will be considerably more. I did not think it was sporting of the Prime Minister this afternoon to attempt to unload so much of the blame on the provinces and municipalities. What he did not say was that many of the provincial and municipal costs result from the fact that this government forced their hands in cost-sharing programs, and the proposal for July 1 next is forcing their hands even more.
I want to come back to the fact that this bill, as the main part of this fourth budget, came about by the most extraordinary procedure in budget history. Its second birth, resulting from Your Honour's ruling, deserves the attention of Shakespeare. The only way to describe it is, "a comedy of errors". Twenty years ago the then minister of finance, Mr. Abbott, brought about budget by radio, then a unique process of bypassing parliament and violating all constitutional precepts. The

uproar which resulted from that technique ought to have laid these odd procedures to final rest. But oh, no, what Mr. Abbott could do the present minister could do better. Last Wednesday afternoon he condescended to tell the house that he intended to propose tax measures. Did he disclose to the house what they were? Not at all. He decided to upstage Mr. Abbott by holding, within an hour of the adjournment of this house, a press conference to tell what he declined to disclose to the people's representatives. Budget by press conference is the new technique for ministers who are "with it". By coincidence, there was a popular television program later that evening and naturally the star of the show was the minister.
Budget by press conference lasted only an hour and a half as the accepted new technique and was replaced by budget by television. So Mr. Abbott, with his old fashioned budget by radio, was passe. The new technique of defiance of parliament, the new way of expressing "parliament be damned" is budget by press conference and budget by television. Finally, this afternoon we have had budget by instalments.
Again, it was the Minister of National Revenue who let the cat out of the bag completely. During the same television interview to which I referred earlier this question was put to the Minister of National Revenue by Mr. Martin:
This week there were announced new fiscal measures after the defeat in the commons of the temporary surtax of 5 per cent. These were announced by means of a press conference: it is rather unusual, let us say, in the traditions and usages of parliament.
The Minister of National Revenue replied:
Yes, it is unusual. It is the first time for a tax to be announced by way of a press conference. But it was as the result of the circumstances which prevailed last week. We were negotiating with several countries and with the United States in particular to stabilize the dollar-
Apparently the minister knew about the negotiations that were going on, although he did not really know the dollar was in difficulty. The Minister of Finance did not disclose the figures to his colleague, apparently.
-and it was absolutely necessary to disclose the new tax to the House of Commons. Since it was a Wednesday, the minister made his presentation in the afternoon without saying precisely what were the nature of the taxes he would levy and he tabled at six o'clock in the House of Commons the budgetary resolutions and he thought that these could lie-
March 12. 1968

I put down "dormant" but it might be translated "undisclosed".
-undisclosed until tomorrow in the afternoon, only the Speaker was inclined to transmit them to the press. Therefore, the Minister of Finance felt he was obliged to make a statement immediately to the press so that it would be patently clear that it was the Minister of Finance who was making the announcement. But he had warned the opposition parties that he was going to do it.
Well, sir, one of the problems with this government is that except for the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who is preoccupied with other matters, they do not have a parliamentarian in their whole kit and caboodle. When they lost Chevrier and Pick-ersgill, and when Martin became an internationalist, they were left without a parliamentarian of any kind. They stumble from one parliamentary crisis to another chiefly because none of them has ever bothered to discover what parliament is all about. I believe, sir, they should remember what Cicero said, that "to stumble twice against the same stone is a proverbial disgrace".
With all the vigour that I can command I deplore their contemptuous treatment of parliament, their cavalier disdain for established budget practices, their scornful arrogance in by-passing this commons chamber. Then, sir, the attempt to present at this one session of parliament a budget proposal so similar in principle, as it is in this bill, to one defeated by this house constitutes a precedent dangerous and intolerable. My comments do not reflect upon Your Honour's ruling but upon the lack of parliamentary understanding by this government. If this house has any role at all which predominates over all others it is as keeper of the purse strings. The precedent set by the Minister of Finance in recent days must be reversed or it will plague our Canadian democracy for long years after all of us have gone to our rewards.
But, sir, odd and objectionable as the procedures have been, even odder still are the proposals themselves. In most aspects the proposals in this bill are far more objectionable than those defeated by this house in Bill No. C-193. I think there are certain principles upon which all members in this house on all sides can agree. All of us appreciate that drastic action is needed to restore confidence domestically and internationally. This government has brought us to that point. All of us agree that defence of the Canadian dollar is a first obligation of parliament and that it must be achieved whatever the side consequences.
Income Tax Act
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
All of us support a major attack upon inflation and its continuous victimizing of every Canadian. Relative stability in the price-cost structure, I submit, is imperative if we are to achieve balanced economic growth. Our trade must be expanded, our productivity greatly enhanced, our industry made adequately competitive.
But, Mr. Speaker, this is the test: will the proposals in this bill achieve any of these agreed objectives? With respect, I submit that they retreat from rather than advance to those objectives. The proposed cure, the 3 per cent surcharge on personal and corporate incomes, will intensify rather than alleviate the fiscal malady. I put it to the house, how can you stabilize prices when you set out deliberately to increase costs of production? That is the government's dilemma. These new tax policies will in fact feed the fires of inflation and in their final impact will bear most heavily on those least able to pay. It is the consumer who will pay for this government's mismanagement.
What I am saying to the house is that what the government is doing is pursuing an inconsistent and self-defeating course. The government seeks to control or at least to stabilize prices; yet by an increase in personal and corporate income taxes it makes inevitable a rise in costs. The government apparently seeks to stabilize wages and salaries; yet it raids the worker's pocketbook, driving him inexorably to seek additional income.
These increased costs of production, inevitable as they will be as a direct result of this bill, will be passed along to the consumer. Those costs which are passed along to the domestic consumer will give impetus to the inflationary spiral. Those passed along to the international consumer will reduce our competitiveness in world trade, enhance our balance of payments difficulties and keep the Canadian dollar in a state of suspense. At the very time when we ought to be exerting a unified national effort to expand our exports, the Minister of Finance is raising our costs in a manner which can only frustrate our export drive. These tax hikes, I submit, will sabotage our trade promotion.
Over last week end in Halifax, I think it was, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) coined the term that the budget proposals would be a "decentive" to industry. He knows they will be as well a "decentive" to trade at the very time when our trade

March 12, 1968
Income Tax Act
promotion should be most aggressive. Why he with his views about balanced budgets and "decentives" remains in this government must be a mystery to all members and indeed to all Canadians. I suggest that he would be doing a national service by insisting upon the immediate acceptance of his resignation so that he can speak his mind freely and easily. The example of the former president of the privy council is there for him to emulate.
So, sir, with this new prices and incomes commission or agency on the one side and the corporate and personal income surcharges on the other, the Minister of Finance is establishing opposing forces that are inevitably set upon a collision course. And, as in so many other matters, the government, being uncertain of its proper course, has set in motion two diametrically opposed forces and now sits back to watch which one will triumph.
The minister's attitude to this situation, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of the following statement by Plato:
Has he not also another object, which is that they may be impoverished by payment of taxes, and thus compelled to devote themselves to their daily wants and therefore less likely to conspire against him?
Are there any alternatives, Mr. Speaker, to the government's present policy? There is one simple alternative that was explicitly presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) last Thursday night. The personal and corporate surcharges are designed to raise $150 million. But the government already has on hand $105 million in refundable corporate tax which it proposed to pay out in this fiscal year and which, under the laws enacted by this parliament, it need not repay before May, 1969. The acceleration of repayment was decided upon by the minister last June, I think it was, when he was in one of his moods which led him to think that the economy needed stimulation and when he thought that he should get some additional money into circulation to prevent slowdown and unemployment. His view of the economy has changed. I suggest he could easily and legally withhold payment instead of imposing an income surcharge.
The minister alleges that this would create problems for the minister of finance in the fiscal year 1969-70. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is only a confession of the inadequacy of his present policies. A budget in this year within reasonable balance would give the new minister of finance in 1969-70 genuine flexibility to

care for the repayment out of growth. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the Minister of Finance that we on this side of the house will not hold it against him at all. We would be quite glad to take our chances on what our budget will be in 1969-70.
If the minister would adopt the Leader of the Opposition's suggestion, Mr. Speaker, the difference to be made up would be $45 to $50 million. Surely, as the Leader of the Opposition said, in a budget of $10J billion it should be possible to save $50 million. It is not as if all the water had already been wrung out of the estimates.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, maybe they are waterlogged.
Last autumn the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) engaged in the greatest propaganda drive of all time to convince the public of their belated conversion to budget restraint. What an heroic battle, we were told, was being waged in Treasury Board to avert increases in expenditures. But when the main estimates were tabled they disclosed what I have pointed out-an 8 per cent rise over the main estimates of one year ago. The alleged "hold the line" policy had become merely a propaganda farce.
All that the Treasury Board had done, Mr. Speaker, was what is done every year, namely, cut back on departmental requests. I think everyone knows, certainly anyone who has sat in government knows, that there is an annual game between departments and Treasury Board. The departments submit considerably more than they expect to receive, believing that whatever they submit Treasury Board will cut them back. This cat and mouse game is as old as the techniques of budgeting. But this year, Mr. Speaker, for the first time the Minister of Finance and the President of Treasury Board made flamboyant boasts about the normal processes of estimating and they claimed virtue for actions which every preceding Treasury Board had considered just good fun.
Now, sir, can there be any further restraints? I point out to the minister that in the summer and autumn of 1962 the late Hon. George Clyde Nowlan and his colleagues on Treasury Board, of whom I was one, managed a reduction of $228 million in a budget of $6J billion without interfering with
March 12, 1968

any essential service. From experience I know how difficult it is, but it can be done and it can be done without loss to the economy and without loss to the essential services to the public.
I want to refer the minister to the tables that appear at page 650 of Hansard for October 18, 1962. He will see there the savings of $228 million. If $228 million can be saved from a $6J billion budget, is it asking too much to save $50 million more from a $10J billion budget, particularly when the minister proposes to save $75 million after the President of the Treasury Board, less than a month ago, assured us that not an additional dollar could be saved from the main estimates? I put it to the Prime Minister that if he would only read the recommendations of the Auditor General and the recommendations in the reports of the public accounts committee of this house he would find a good many ways to take him a long way to the objectives he has named.

Sir, there are times when I wish the minister would frame and put on his desk, so that he could see it every hour, this quotation from a message that President Grover Cleveland gave to congress:
When more of the people's sustenance is exacted through the form of taxation than is necessary to meet the just obligations of government and expenses of its economical administration, such exaction becomes ruthless extortion and a violation of the fundamental principles of a free government.

speechtext:
When this government came to office less than five years ago spending was at a rate of about $6 billion per annum. Now, as a result of what the former distinguished Superintendent of Insurance, K.R. MacGregor, described as the "spend-yourself-rich" theory of government, spending exceeds $10.25 billion. By the end of the next fiscal year it will exceed $10.5 billion. Some of Mr. MacGregor's comments in his address to the last annual meeting of the Mutual Life Assurance Company of Canada are directly relevant to this bill and the budget policy it represents, and I quote them:
Earlier, I referred to the "spend-yourself-rich" theory of government. At this point, I should like to suggest the desirability of abandoning as well the "spend-yourself-popular" theory of government in favour of policies more attuned to the wishes of most Canadians. Political leaders seem to 27053-4751

have been proceeding on the assumption that Canadians want a paternalistic government, but I am convinced that a majority want first, good government, in order to lead the country out of confusion and uncertainty,-

The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) asked me to be honest. I am trying to be honest.
