There is no way to avoid this. I do not propose to present my arguments on any basis other than a recognition of that fact in a modern society.
There are other areas, however, in which serious cuts in expenditures can be made in addition to cutting down on waste and extravagance. There are such things as some of those suggested by the Auditor General and by the Glassco commission. We think there are also other ways in which to cut expenditures. We have indicated these time and time again to the government. We believe Canada should stop wasting money on defence expenditures that are of no value to the international community and of no value to Canada's national interests. Every penny spent on NORAD-if my memory serves me correctly the amount is about $130 million-is a total and absolute waste because NORAD was created to meet a threatened manned bomber attack the danger of which disappeared if it ever existed at all. Most of our defence expenditures under NATO are now

useless because the situation in Europe is entirely changed. I do not wish to go into the details of this. My friend and colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) did so the other day.
The international situation for which NATO was created in 1948-49 no longer exists. The threat of Soviet attack in Europe has certainly receded and I hope with all my heart has disappeared. Statements by representatives of all the members of NATO and the recent investigation have shown that everybody is agreed that the role of NATO should be changed from that of a military alliance to that of an organization to negotiate with the Warsaw pact countries solutions to European political problems. These, therefore, are the areas in which the government could bring about cuts in expenditures of hundreds of millions of dollars without affecting any issue of principle or welfare internationally or nationally. The right hon. Prime Minister recognized this but then said, if I remember his words correctly, that this would mean becoming an uncommitted nation.
I do not see what right-I was first inclined to use rather stronger language-the Prime Minister had to say that. France has withdrawn its military participation in NATO and is by no means an uncommitted nation. There are other nations in Europe which are not part of the military NATO machine and they are by no means uncommitted nations. We are not suggesting for one moment that Canada should be anything other than a nation concerned with the welfare and progress of the democracies and the democratic objectives which all of us in this parliament are determined to preserve and expand. That does not mean, however, that we must participate in huge military expenditures that are of no value. That is the case in respect of the expenditures to which I have referred.

Why is Canada pretty confident that we can hold the dollar with care but without too much trouble? It is basically because the economies of North America are strong. Our resources are many and our economies are rich. That is why we can do what a poor economy like Britain's, which requires a great deal of modernization and a great deal of attention, was unable to do.
These are the things we should do to protect our currency. We must manage the economy properly by planning properly, not planning the way the Minister of Finance and his advisors have been doing or, as my leader

The biggest surprise, judging by the nature of its work and the modesty of its achievements, has been provided by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Its annual budget has leaped from about $179 million
Income Tax Act
five years ago to a staggering $403 million, an increase of $224 million in five years, or just about 127 per cent. It is true some savings have been made, but they were marginal savings at the expense of services to the taxpayer, not on such items as staff, travelling expenses, telephone calls, office rent and so on. Public works, transportation and defence services have all been pared. Indian and Eskimo peoples will have to make do with an even lower standard of medical and welfare assistance than in the past.
If the twins of finance and revenue had used a sharper paring knife the bill now before us would have been unnecessary. Recently the Minister of Finance said a great deal about the critical situation in which this country suddenly finds itself, leaving the impression that it is all due to outside influences beyond our control, and that he and his fellow ministers are waging an heroic battle to save Canada. He solemnly tells us it is the patriotic duty of all Canadians to refrain from criticism and do what he asks them to do.
Mr. Speaker, for the past five years the opposition has been pointing out to the government that its inability to control expenditures was running the country into trouble. We have tried to indicate long-range policies and demonstrate the need for better control in the economic sphere. The government's advisers have told them the same things. But hon. gentlemen opposite ignored their advisers as they ignored the opposition. Now they have landed in the economic soup as a result of their own floundering efforts, and they come crying to the people to help them out.
In conclusion I would simply say that the illustrations I have given are not all new. They have been given by others over a considerable period. What I have stated has been said by every reputable financial writer and newspaperman in Canada for the past year or more. People have lost confidence in this government. Today there is an outflow of millions of dollars on the part of Canadians who are selling Canadian securities and purchasing United States securities. This is shocking, but it has been going on for some time. People are doing this because they say they lose their money through inflation in the United States only half as fast as they are currently losing it in Canada, and there are some other advantages.

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), addressing an FAO conference in Rome, had this to say with reference to Canadian taxpayers:
If they lose faith in the efficiency of our endeavours, if they come to believe that their taxes are but adding to the bureaucracy or to the pile of papers in some murky vault, they will lose the will to participate.
These are true words and I commend the hon. gentleman for saying them. I wish he had been able to persuade his fellow members in the cabinet to take them to heart. I have not lost faith in Canada or lost my confidence in this great country, far from it. But I along with millions of other Canadians have lost confidence in this government and I propose to vote against this bill.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBLE WITHDRAWAL OF CANADIAN FORCES FROM NORAD AS MEASURE OF ECONOMY
speechtext:
The other day I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question which is being asked increasingly often by the people of Canada, and it was this:
As an aid to curtailing unnecessary spending and saving the Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars, will the government consider withdrawing Canada's participation in NORAD?
The other day I got no answer. Yesterday, my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) asked a question on the same subject in an effort to get the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to guarantee that parliament would have an opportunity to discuss the NORAD agreement before it comes up for renewal on May 12, so that the Canadian people may know what they are being committed to.
The Prime Minister replied in these words:
No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot give that assurance. The government will have to take its responsibilities and then submit its decision to the house as is normally done in connection with these matters.
(Mr. Hales.1
DEBATES	March 12, 1968
I do not know whether this is normal or not, but I believe the people of Canada ought to be given an opportunity to discuss the NORAD agreement in all its aspects before they are committed to what will be an inexorable ten-year contract with the United States. The agreement comes up only once every ten years.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
There is no doubt that when the new NORAD agreement is submitted to Canada it will contain some far reaching changes. The Canadian people are very worried at the prospect of the government signing the new NORAD agreement before we have an opportunity of knowing what its new provisions will be, and what Canada will be committed to for the next ten years.
For some years now the New Democratic party, of which I am a member, has believed and has urged that Canada should withdraw from NORAD. I shall briefly give our reasons for urging this. First we consider that NORAD is a worthless defence against a threat that never came off, the threat in the minds of United States military commanders that the U.S.S.R. would build up huge bomber fleets to use against this continent. In this context NORAD today is a museum piece along with the Maginot line. Neither has provided any security because they were not designed to meet developments that actually took place.
Second, we want to withdraw from NORAD because every year NORAD is a waste of $130 million of the taxpayers' hard earned money. At a time when the government is scraping every little bit it can from small taxpayers, it would be a big relief to the taxpayers of this country to save $130 million a year on something which is an expensive and worthless activity.
Third, we want to withdraw from NORAD because the money we could save by so doing we could use for many useful and necessary things in Canada, such as housing, medicare, and pensions, to mention only three. By providing money for these things we would do a great deal for the internal security and wellbeing of the country when, as I say, NORAD in its present form has been proven obsolete.
Fourth, if we stay in NORAD we shall be drawn closer and closer into the net of United States plans for continental defence, involving huge expenditures on new interceptor aircraft and other military hardware, of which we
March 12, 1968	COMMONS
know very little and of which we will know nothing more until the government has signed, sealed and delivered the new agreement which will commit us for another ten year period. We believe that this sort of things is far too dangerous for Canada. It means that we are choosing Canada as the battlefield for a nuclear war between powerful super powers, and I don't mean just the United States and the U.S.S.R. because there will be other super powers within the next ten years. I think that would be a very strange form of protection for the people of our country.
In the fifth place, if we mean what we say, Canada should throw her support not behind a regional alliance such as NORAD but behind the United Nations. We should work more forcefully than ever for a United Nations peace keeping force free from domination by powerful super powers.
How can we tell the people of the other countries of the world that we are free from entangling alliances, from set points of view, and from imperialism of all kinds if we are tied up tight to the Pentagon? Having seen what is going on over in Asia, and in Viet Nam in particular during the last few years, I think we should be taking this heaven-sent chance provided by the renewal of the NORAD agreement to get out of that entanglement. The United States has got deeper and deeper into that situation over in Asia, and I do not think we should allow Canada to be dragged into the morass that is the war in Viet Nam.
I urge that the Canadian people be given a chance through parliament to debate this treaty before it is signed on May 12, and I believe that those Canadian people, through the Canadian parliament, should decide at this time to withdraw altogether from NORAD.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated in his statement to the standing committee on external affairs last Thursday, the government considers that there is a continuing threat to North America from manned bombers which it would be irresponsible for it to ignore. For this reason the government believes we should co-operate with the United States in the defence of the continent as we have done in one way or another since the beginning of the second world war. If co-operation between the air defence forces of Canada and the United States against the continuing
DEBATES	7571
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion bomber threat is to be effective it is necessary to have a single air defence plan and an integrated command and control system. This requirement has been satifactorily met by NORAD for the past ten years.
The government is now in the process of negotiation and consideration of the existing agreement which expires in May. The financial burden of maintaining the NORAD command structure is borne substantially by the United States. The cost to Canada for defence against bombers arises largely out of Canada's contribution of forces and equipment to this joint task. These costs would thus be incurred regardless of whether or not NORAD existed, unless we permitted the United States to assume controlling responsibility for the defence of Canada against bombers and, indeed, for the surveillance of Canadian air space. Such a surrender of sovereignty the government is not prepared to contemplate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, as I have done on several occasions in recent months, I asked a question about the Canadian attitude toward and participation in efforts to bring about a cessation of the war in Nigeria which has gone on for many months, a war which is called the forgotten war and one which arrests little interest and receives little space in the newspapers. This is a profound and appalling tragedy, marked as wars always are with hatred, destruction and death. I should like to see more interest and more initiative taken by this country, which has contributed so much to the development of the modern commonwealth of autonomous states. We should not wait until the explosion becomes more devastating and the dangers more threatening; nor should we wait until great power competition-and it is there as in other wars -escalates explosively.
In Canada, unfortunately, we have little thoughtful journalism devoted to an in-depth coverage of international affairs. Only the sensational ever gains attention. It would be revealing if one could enumerate the small number of dispatches emanating from or dealing with Nigeria in the months since the war began. So it is parliament which must show the initiative in this terribly important matter.
On February 9, in answer to a question of mine the Prime Minister indicated that he thought this would be a subject he would
March 12, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion discuss with the British Prime Minister. After the visit it became clear that this question was not discussed. If our belief in the commonwealth is to be more than tokenism, surely it is incumbent upon us to concern ourselves with, and exert with other commonwealth states a powerful pressure for peace in this strife torn part of the world.
We do not have to assess blame; it would be unlikely that all wrong is one side and all good is on the other. But if we circumscribe and inhibit all our actions and responses by the declaration that we recognize only Nigeria and refuse even to hear the voice of Biafra, we are in fact being neutral on one side in this terrible conflict.
The United Kingdom has certainly been neutral on one side. It is providing arms to Lagos, a practice which Lord Goodman in a House of Lords debate recently described as "wholly inappropriate, wholly shameful and wholly wrong", and I agree with him wholly. This is scarcely a helpful attitude on the part of the senior member of the commonwealth. The government in providing arms to Lagos has joined company with the Soviet union. Surely if there is any vitality in the commonwealth there should be joint action in the first instance to put a stop to this arms flow.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Out of Biafra there are trickling horrible stories of atrocities approaching the range of genocide. As the Archbishop of Canterbury said in the debate to which I have referred, "Biafra people have suffered the most terrible violence". There are serious estimates from thoughtful people of massacres of as many as 30,000 men, women and children in the eastern provinces of Nigeria. As one well known African expert has said, surely before long Biafra will end up being half cemetery and half concentration camp.
With such dreadful statistics coming out, should not one of the first orders of the day be the dispatch of a fact finding commission to get to the bottom of the situation. Surely Canada will do its part in this regard. After that might come a more important exercise. If a cessation of hostilities could be obtained, and it must, there could be a dispatch of a peace keeping force. This would have to be agreeable to both sides, but what a challenge this would be to the commonwealth states; if men from the far flung members of this unique and interesting association of nations could go to that troubled area and maintain the peace in that country, which brought such

great hopes to all believers in the commonwealth and all people interested in Africa just a few years ago. I would like to see Canada take the lead in this regard and turn our proclamations of affection for the commonwealth into concrete action to restore peace and to bring about a settlement in that area, so events could move to that kind of climax, just as in some of those other dreadful situations in other areas about which we have been belatedly concerned. This is the sort of thing I feel we should reach out for, before events drag us in. Surely farsightedness is a part of statesmanship, and surely our position in the commonwealth requires statesmanship of this order.

Here, Mr. Speaker, is an outline of the efforts of the Canadian government to bring about a peaceful settlement in Nigeria. I should first of all express, as we have expressed before, the government's deep concern at the tragic events taking place in this fellow commonwealth country which has the largest population of any country in Africa and potentially one of the brightest futures of any of the new nations. Canada's close association with Nigeria since its independence has been a source of great satisfaction to us; our commonwealth ties are strong and we have been able to provide capital and technical assistance to the Nigerian people as a concrete expression of our friendship and our desire to see the country develop further as a strong and responsible member of the community of nations.
The civil turmoil which has been taking place in Nigeria since the middle of last year has, as I said, been a matter of concern to us, and we have felt called upon to give expression to that concern as well as our genuine willingness to be of what assistance we can in helping the Nigerians to find means of solving Nigeria's problems. Other countries and organizations including the organization of African unity, have voiced similar concern. The Nigerian federal military government has made it clear that it considers Nigeria's problems to be of an internal character, to be resolved by Nigerians themselves without outside interference. We naturally respect this position as well as Nigeria's status as a fully independent nation, but we have taken every occasion to impress on the Nigerian federal leaders our concern with the situation in their country, and our hope that it will be possible
March 12. 1968
to reach a negotiated settlement of Nigeria's problems. These views were expressed by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs during the centennial visit to Canada last October of Admiral Wey, who represented the the federal military government, and the visit in December of the Nigerian commissioner for external affairs, Dr. Arikpo.
The eastern region of Nigeria has declared itself in secession from the rest of the country and has used military and other means within its control to try to enforce this declaration. Neither the Canadian government nor any other government has recognized this secessionist regime, and we have relations only with the central authorities of the federal government at Lagos. None the less, when we express our hope, publicly and to the government at Lagos, that a negotiated settlement may be found, we mean particularly that means may be found to resolve the differences between the federal authorities and the eastern Nigerians who have declared themselves to be in secession.
It has seemed to the government that while other organizations might be able to afford assistance to the Nigerians in their search for a settlement, the commonwealth through its secretary general is at present the best placed to provide help when needed. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will only keep hon. members in orbit for a short while this evening. This is not meant to refer to the eloquent plea of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) on behalf of commonwealth action in Africa, to which I heartily subscribe, but it refers to the question I ventured this afternoon about the space program of this country.
My question was prompted by a number of press reports today, particularly in Montreal and Toronto papers, of a meeting of the Canadian Aeronautics and Space Institute which was held in Montreal. It was attended
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion by experts from universities, industry and government. Please note that civil servants were present. It was stated quite frankly that this meeting was held to get federal authorities to act quickly in establishing a space agency. It was also stated that the purpose of the meeting was to complain about the absence of a national space agency for Canada.
Some history is necessary to explain my point. I should like to refer to the statement which was made in the so-called Chapman committee report of February 1967 which said:
The need for use by Canada of communications satellites for domestic communications is clearly established, and there is a risk that ultimate control over the specification, supply, and operation of the space segment of a communications satellite system may not reside in Canada.
Perhaps the record should contain some of the references because this will be a continuing matter. The first reference, with which I have had some connection after the estimates of last year, was a question which was asked of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) on November 17 about the meeting he had in the United States on the matter of a space program and satellite operation. The minister did not say there was direct discussion on this subject but he offered some hope when he said this whole matter was presently under discussion by the government and decisions will be announced in the not too distant future.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
On December 14, 1967, I asked another question pointing out the implications of his space and satellite matter in connection with the Bell Telephone bill. At that time the minister said, as reported on page 5411 of Hansard:
If it were felt essential this matter could be given consideration, because the government has made considerable progress in its plans in respect of commercial satellites.
He went on to say that it might be possible for the committee to look into it. Well, we passed the Bell Telephone bill and the matter was not discussed. We are at the time when the civil servants have presented their study. Last January, two consortiums were formed, one being the so-called Soble consortium, which has made its request. We have a new one now that is called the Canadian communications satellite system, which includes the trans-Canada telephone system and C.N.-C.P. Telecommunications. A report has

March 12, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion already come forward and the minister has had his meetings in the United States. The deputy minister has told the broadcasting committee that some first steps have been taken, but we still have not received any definite word or a progress report.
I feel very sincerely, Mr. Speaker, that Canada must have its own space program, and I of course include satellites in this. I think that is in the national interest. It is important, even necessary, to co-operate in some aspects of this program with the United States and even with Russia. However, we must go forward and have this program in the interests of this great nation where geography problems are so tremendous. It will help our defence and many of our industries. One can think of television and other aspects of the communications field that will be affected. It is a broad subject and I will not get into it tonight. I merely ask now the question that I felt was not completely answered this afternoon:	What progress
report can the government give in this regard? At the same time, I urge the government to get moving, because we are losing our place in this very important international field, as was pointed out at this meeting yesterday which was reported in the newspapers this morning.
